narrative:
The model predicted a 64.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile (bottom 10%) of your class in Year 3 is well below the average of roughly the fifth or sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low academic standing in later years signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction toward passing. At 35, your score is only modestly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, so the model saw this as a mild positive factor. However, it was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class ranking.

Family income was the third most important factor and also nudged the outcome toward failure. Being in the middle-income bracket is fairly common, yet the model still interpreted it as slightly increasing risk compared with the higher-income brackets that dominate among accepted applicants.

Taken together, your relatively low class standing in Year 3 outweighed the decent LSAT and created a failure probability high enough to result in rejection.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a structured bar-prep program, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. Improving your upper-year performance and LSAT would directly address the factors that most hurt your application. (248 words)
